# What Paul Graham Means by "Do Things that Don't Scale"

Based on Paul Graham's essay from July 2013, here's what he means:

## The Core Concept

**Startups don't grow automatically.** Graham challenges the common misconception that if you build a better product, customers will naturally find you. Instead, he argues that **founders must actively "push" their startups to get them going** through deliberate, labor-intensive effort.

He uses a helpful metaphor: like the hand cranks needed to start car engines before electric starters existed, startups require an initial, separate, and laborious process to get momentum. Once the engine is running, it keeps going—but getting it started requires manual effort.

## The Practical Reality

The most concrete example Graham provides is **recruiting users manually**. Nearly all startups have to do this at the start—personally reaching out to potential users one by one, rather than relying on scalable marketing or organic growth.

## Why This Matters

The advice directly counters the false belief that startups either "take off or don't" based solely on product quality. The truth is: **startups take off because founders make them take off** through personal, unscalable actions.

This is so foundational to Graham's philosophy that when asked about growth strategies, he famously deflected by saying: "go read that [essay], because I can't remember everything I said."
